events.title: Earliest tattoo in the Americas (Chinchorro)
events.descr: The Chinchorro were famous for detailed mummification, practised from 7,000 BC; around 2000 BC their mummies change from black manganese to red.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Chinchorro mummies and Early tattoo

events.title: The Chinchorro culture ends
events.descr: Set around 3500 BP. Influences from the Andean Plateau lead to farming around 3,000 BP, and later groups no longer mummify their dead.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Chinchorro mummies and Later developments

events.title: The Casimiroid peoples settle the Caribbean
events.descr: They precede the Ortoiroid peoples.

events.title: Ortoiroid peoples move into the Antilles
events.descr: Known for stone tools but without ceramics; they bury their dead beneath shell middens. They settle Saint Kitts from 2000 BC to 400 BC and in most places disappear by about 400 BC (the Coroso culture survives until 200 AD).

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Settlement patterns, Culture and Decline

events.title: Saladoid potters reach the Lesser Antilles and Puerto Rico
events.descr: Farmers and potters living in settled villages, believed to have spoken an Arawakan language; they displace the pre-ceramic Ortoiroid culture.

events.title: Okunev stelae and the first bronze of north-eastern Central Asia
events.descr: The Okunev raise monumental stelae at gravesites and, with the neighbouring Samus culture, produce the first bronze in north-eastern Central Asia. Images of two-wheeled carts appear at the end of the 3rd millennium BC. They raise livestock, and closely interact with the successors of the Andronovo circle.

sources.sourceLocation: Dating, Monumental steles, Metallurgy, Wheeled transport, Livestock and Related cultures

events.title: Glazkov hunters and fishers
events.descr: An economy of hunting, fishing and gathering, with copper knives and bronze fishing hooks; contemporary with the Andronovo culture to the west.

events.title: Ymyyakhtakh culture
events.descr: Bronze ware is frequent in its burial grounds; after 1,700 BC it is believed to spread east.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Description and Associated sites

events.title: Karasuk bronzes and chariots reach Shang China
events.descr: Karasuk farmers practise metallurgy on a large scale. Many Shang (13th–11th centuries BCE) and Zhou bronze blades derive from Karasuk designs, and Wu (2013) traces Shang chariots and their equipment to the Karasuk culture.

events.title: Deer stones raised in Mongolia
events.descr: Large standing stelae renowned for lively images of deer, part of a pastoral tradition of stone burial mounds; deer-stone art is earlier than the first Scythian sites such as Arzhan by 300 to 500 years. The oldest dated stones, in Khovsgol, are of about 1300 BC.

events.title: Slab-grave culture replaces the deer-stone culture
events.descr: In central and eastern Mongolia. The two cultures had been adjacent and essentially contemporaneous; slab-grave art shares many features with Karasuk and Tagar.

events.title: Tagar culture: royal kurgans and bronze-smelting
events.descr: One of the largest centres of bronze-smelting in ancient Eurasia. Huge royal kurgans are fenced by stone plaques with stelae at the corners; their animal art is very like that of the Scythians of southern European Russia. Usually considered descendants of the Andronovo culture.

events.title: Karuo: the first farmers on the Tibetan Plateau
events.descr: The oldest permanent settlement in Tibet and the earliest evidence for agriculture on the plateau, growing foxtail millet; its pottery resembles that of Majiayao sites. The residents abandon Karuo suddenly around 1750 BC.

events.title: Nyatri Tsenpo, first Yarlung king (traditional date)
events.descr: Some Tibetan texts give 126 BC, others 414 BC. Tibetan texts name the kingdom of Zhangzhung (c. 500 BC–625 AD) as the precursor of later Tibetan kingdoms.

events.title: Gandhara grave culture: the Swat graveyards
events.descr: Large graveyards appear in northern Gandhara close to the end of the second millennium BCE; the inhumations of c. 1200–900 BCE come from a period in which iron technology was introduced. Parpola links it with the Cemetery H culture in Punjab.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Location and Indo-Aryan migrations

source.sourceLocation: lead (no burials of this kind after 800 BCE)

events.title: Early Iron Age in South India
events.descr: Sites such as Hallur and Adichanallur are generally dated to around 1000 BCE; the Iron Age partly corresponds with the megalithic cultures of South India. Much earlier radiocarbon dates from Sivagalai and Mayiladumparai are disputed.

events.title: Sri Lankan cinnamon in Egypt
events.descr: Cinnamon, native to Sri Lanka, was in use in Ancient Egypt, suggesting trading links with the island.

events.title: A large settlement at Anuradhapura
events.descr: Founded before 900 BC and covering 10 ha by 800 BC. In the protohistoric period (1000–500 BCE) Sri Lanka is culturally united with southern India.

events.title: The African humid period ends: the Sahara dries
events.descr: Considered the greatest environmental transition of the Holocene in northern Africa; people move to places such as the Nile Valley and Mesopotamia, and the change is linked to the birth of Ancient Egyptian civilization. The end comes in several steps; by 2,700 years ago the central Sahara is a desert.

source.sourceLocation: End ('an ending date of 5,500 years before present is often used')

events.title: Pan-tropical drought about 4,000 years ago
events.descr: A major environmental change accompanied by the collapse of ancient civilizations and severe drought in Africa, Asia and the Middle East; some count this step (the 4.2-kiloyear event) as the true end of the humid period. Nile discharge decreases noticeably.

events.title: Herding reaches East Africa
events.descr: Livestock arrived in northern Africa around 8000 BP; as the Green Sahara dried, herders spread into the Nile Valley and reached the Turkana Basin around 5000 BP (3000 BC).

events.title: Herders reach the highlands of Kenya and Tanzania
events.descr: South Cushitic-speaking pastoralists who buried their dead in cairns settled first in the Kenyan lowlands (5,200–3,300 ybp). These early Cushitic speakers largely disappeared after the Bantu expansion.

events.title: First settlement of Palau
events.descr: Settled by Austronesian peoples, most likely from what is now the Philippines or Indonesia. The page’s history section places it between the 3rd and 2nd millennia BCE.

source.sourceLocation: Early history ('between the 3rd and 2nd millennia BCE')

events.title: Jericho, the first town
events.descr: Jericho is thought to be the world’s first town; it is the type site of the Pre-Pottery Neolithic A and B, defined by Kathleen Kenyon. PPNA people lived in tiny circular mud-brick dwellings, cultivated crops and hunted wild game, without pottery. The PPNA succeeds the Natufian culture.

events.title: The Tower of Jericho
events.descr: One of the world’s oldest towers and oldest stone buildings, built against the wall inside the town at the end of the PPNA; its construction is estimated to have taken 11,000 working days. Barkai and Liran suggest astronomical and social purposes.

events.title: Goats, sheep, pigs and cattle domesticated
events.descr: About 9000 BCE for goats and sheep, 8500 BCE for pigs and 8000 BCE for cattle. Çayönü is possibly the place where the pig was first domesticated.

events.title: Plastered skulls of the Levant
events.descr: Made in the Pre-Pottery Neolithic B, they are some of the oldest forms of art in the Middle East. In this period houses become rectilinear with thick white plaster floors; plaster work may have led to the discovery of pottery.

events.title: ’Ain Ghazal and its plaster statues
events.descr: At its prime around 7000 BCE some 3,000 people live here, four to five times contemporary Jericho. Its 32 plaster figures, some two-headed, are among the oldest large statues ever found. After 6500 BC the population drops to about one sixth.

events.title: The 8.2-kiloyear climate event
events.descr: Approximately 8,200 years before the present. At ’Ain Ghazal the population drops sharply after 6500 BC, a decline its page links to this event.

events.title: Ghassulian villages: copper and painted walls
events.descr: Mixed farming hamlets with remarkable polychrome wall paintings (including the "Ghassulian Star"); they smelted copper and buried their dead in stone dolmens. The culture correlates closely with the Amratian of Egypt.

events.title: Göbekli Tepe: circular enclosures with stone pillars
events.descr: Popularly called the world’s first temples: at least 20 large enclosures with stone pillars, carved with reliefs of animals, built by hunter-gatherers who supplemented their diet with early domesticated cereal. The earliest exposed structures date to 9500–9000 BCE. Karahan Tepe and other nearby sites share its architecture and iconography.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Dawn of village life and Chronology

events.title: Copper and malachite workshop at Çayönü
events.descr: A specialised workshop found in 2026. Çayönü belongs to the Taş Tepeler tradition of Göbekli Tepe and is an early example of agriculture, implemented from the 9th millennium BC.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Archaeology and Origin of domestication

events.title: Çatalhöyük
events.descr: A settlement of domestic buildings with no obvious public buildings, rebuilt in 18 successive layers and flourishing around 7000 BC. Vivid murals include what is frequently cited as the world’s oldest map; over 2,500 clay figurines have been found, and some skulls were plastered and painted. About 600–800 people lived there in an average year of the middle phase (6700–6500 BC).

events.title: Hassuna: the first farmers of northern Mesopotamia
events.descr: By around 6000 BC people had moved into the foothills of northernmost Mesopotamia, making cream-slipped pottery painted in red; Umm Dabaghiyah is believed to have the region’s earliest pottery.

events.title: Halaf culture: painted pottery and the first stamp seals
events.descr: The earliest systematic plant motifs in Near Eastern prehistoric art and the earliest known stamp seals in the Near East; Halaf-influenced material is found throughout Greater Mesopotamia. Most scholars see its end as a Halafian adoption of the Ubaid culture.

events.title: Samarra culture: early irrigation
events.descr: Irrigation and flax at Tell es-Sawwan show a prosperous settled culture; it is best known for fine pottery decorated with stylised animals, and was the precursor of the Ubaid period.

events.title: Tell el-’Oueili: the oldest known site in southern Mesopotamia
events.descr: Its Ubaid 0 levels are older than those of Eridu. The earliest settlements south of Uruk date to the eighth millennium BC.

source.sourceLocation: Climate ('the Ubaid 0 levels at Oueili (6500-6000 BC)')

events.title: Eridu founded
events.descr: Built on a virgin sand dune, it was traditionally the earliest city of southern Mesopotamia in the Sumerian King List. Eighteen superimposed mudbrick temples stand at the site, and twelve clay tokens from its Ubaid levels are precursors of proto-cuneiform.

events.title: Chogha Golan: domesticated emmer wheat
events.descr: The earliest record of long-term plant management in Iran: people lived mainly on wild plants and hunting, and domesticated emmer appears about 2,000 years after settlement began (around 9,800 BP).

events.title: Ganj Dareh: the earliest domesticated goats
events.descr: The earliest evidence for goat domestication in the world; two-row barley is the only domesticated crop found so far.

events.title: Jeitun: the oldest arable farming in Central Asia
events.descr: Villagers kept sheep and goats that were brought already domesticated, and built with sun-dried clay blocks. The culture may have begun before 7000 BC.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Jeitun culture, Agriculture and Excavations

events.title: Chogha Mish settled
events.descr: Its Early Susiana period is contemporary with Ubaid 1 in southern Mesopotamia. The main monumental building is destroyed in the early 5th millennium BC, and the site declines about 4400 BC.

events.title: Tepe Sialk settled
events.descr: Tombs of Sialk I contain pottery. Later, silver metallurgy at the site is radiocarbon-dated to 3660–3520 B.C., and Sialk IV has links with Uruk-period Mesopotamia and with Proto-Elamite Susa.

sources.sourceLocation: History, Sialk I, Sialk IV and Silver metallurgy

events.title: Shahr-e Sukhteh founded
events.descr: In Period I it has connections with the Proto-Elamite cities of Khuzestan and Fars; later it is in contact with the pre-Harappan centres of the Indus valley.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, Archaeology, Period I and Period II

events.title: Shulaveri–Shomu: the earliest winemaking
events.descr: The earliest evidence for winemaking and grape cultivation in the Near East. Goats, sheep, cattle, pigs and dogs are kept from the earliest phase; around 5900 BC villagers at Gadachrili divert a river, the oldest water management in the Caucasus.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Subsistence and Earliest grapes

events.title: Nabta Playa: herders and early pottery
events.descr: One of the earliest sites of the Nubian Neolithic. People begin to make pottery locally around 6800 BC, and larger settlements appear by the 7th millennium BC; domesticated cattle reach northeast Africa in the late 7th millennium BC.

events.title: Nabta Playa stone circle
events.descr: May be among the world’s earliest known archaeoastronomical devices; a megalith period follows, about 4500 to 3600 BC. Researchers see the site as an early evolution of the Hathor cult.

sources.sourceLocation: Astronomical observation, Recent research and Religious ties

events.title: Faiyum A: the first farming villages of Lower Egypt
events.descr: Weaving is evidenced for the first time; goats and sheep had been introduced from the Neolithic Levant around 6000 BCE. Neolithic settlements appear all over Egypt from around 6210 BC.

sources.sourceLocation: Faiyum A culture and Neolithic anthropology

events.title: Merimde culture
events.descr: Cattle, sheep, goats and pigs are kept; its later phase corresponds to the Faiyum A and Badari cultures.

events.title: Badarian culture: the earliest farming in Upper Egypt
events.descr: They keep cattle, sheep and goats, give livestock and dogs ceremonial burial, and make black-topped pottery; the Western Desert was probably the most influential of its sources.

source.sourceLocation: lead ('might have already emerged by 5000 BC')

events.title: Naqada I (Amratian)
events.descr: Obsidian and a little gold are imported from Nubia, and charcoal from Nekhen tombs is cedar from Lebanon. Werner Kaiser’s chronology starts the Naqada culture c. 4000 BC.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead and Commerce and crafts

events.title: Capsian hunters of Algeria and Tunisia
events.descr: An Epipalaeolithic tradition whose first phase overlaps the African humid period, in open savanna; they hunted game from aurochs and hartebeest to hares and snails. Historical linguists tentatively link it with the earliest Afroasiatic speakers in Africa.

events.title: Gobero: the oldest cemetery in the Sahara
events.descr: Kiffian fisher-gatherers, makers of pottery with wavy lines, live beside a large lake in the Green Sahara (7500–3500 BCE); after a gap (6200–5200 BCE) Tenerian people herd domesticated cattle there. At least 182 burials include a man buried with a turtle carapace and a grave decorated with flowers.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Site, Excavations, Kiffian culture, Tenerian culture and Burials

events.title: The Dufuna canoe, Africa’s oldest boat
events.descr: The second-oldest known boat in the world, after the Pesse canoe.

events.title: Star Carr
events.descr: Britain’s oldest structure and the earliest known carpentry in Europe; a pendant found in 2015 is thought to be the oldest Mesolithic art in Britain. Occupation lasts about 800 years.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Settlement and artefacts and Post-2000 investigations

events.title: Maglemosian hunters of the north
events.descr: They appear to have domesticated the dog; bark huts survive, and they fished with a characteristic leister spear.

events.title: Lepenski Vir: fish-faced sculptures
events.descr: The late architectural phase, with numerous fish sculptures with human-like faces. From about 7500 BC Early European Farmers arriving from Asia Minor begin to settle the Balkans and the Danube valley.

events.title: Farming reaches Greece
events.descr: Neolithic material culture came to Europe via western Anatolia. Farming spread from the Aegean to Britain in about 2,500 years (6500–4000 BC), at about 1 km a year; the Sesklo culture is called the earliest known Neolithic culture of Europe.

events.title: Starčevo–Körös–Criș farmers
events.descr: Dated by the infobox; the body gives about 5500–4500, and other sources 6200–5200.

events.title: Cardial Ware farmers spread along the Mediterranean
events.descr: Pottery impressed with cockle shells, from Epirus and Corfu (6400–6200 BC) to the Atlantic coasts of Portugal and Morocco; it reaches Iberia in probably no more than 100–200 years. Its people were closely related to the earlier Neolithic farmers of north-west Anatolia.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, The Mediterranean Neolithic and Genetics

events.title: Linear Pottery farmers spread across central Europe
events.descr: Appearing about 5600–5400 BC on the middle Danube, the culture spreads about 1,500 km in 360 years, building long houses.

events.title: Vinča culture: early copper smelting and Vinča symbols
events.descr: It has the earliest known example of copper smelting, and its symbols are conjectured by some to be the earliest proto-writing.

events.title: Varna Necropolis: the oldest gold
events.descr: The oldest gold treasure and jewellery in the world, dated by radiocarbon in 2006.

events.title: The Carnac stones
events.descr: A dense collection of megalithic sites near the south coast of Brittany; the tumulus at Tumiac was raised between 4790 and 4530 BC, contemporary with the rich Varna burials.

events.title: Mehrgarh: the earliest farming in South Asia
events.descr: A farming village of unbaked mud brick; barley and zebu cattle were probably domesticated locally, and drilled teeth show proto-dentistry. Its dating is debated (Jarrige: before 7000 BCE; Mutin and Zazzo: 5250–4650 BCE). Its culture later migrated into the Indus Valley and became the Indus Valley Civilisation.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Period I, Lifestyle, History and Notes

events.title: Bhirrana’s earliest levels (Hakra ware)
events.descr: Charcoal from the lowest levels gave 7570–7180 BCE, said to predate the Indus Valley civilisation; other excavators date these levels much later (Garge: from about 4600 BCE).

events.title: Lahuradewa: early rice and pottery in the Ganges plain
events.descr: Rice from Period IA is AMS-dated to the 7th millennium BCE, but whether it was cultivated or gathered wild is debated; its pottery is the oldest evidence of ceramics in the Indian Subcontinent. Irfan Habib gives 4220–2879 BCE.

events.title: Domesticated rice at Pengtoushan
events.descr: Rice residues carbon-dated to 8200–7800 BC show that rice had been domesticated; by 4000 BC evidence of rice domestication in the region is abundant.

events.title: Jiahu: bone flutes, carved signs and fermented drink
events.descr: The earliest Peiligang site: 33 flutes carved from crane wing bones, eleven pictographic symbols on tortoise shell and bone, foxtail millet and rice, alcohol fermented from rice, honey, grapes and hawthorn, and the earliest common-carp aquaculture. A flood ends it around 5700 BC.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Inscriptions, Agriculture and Pottery and alcohol production

events.title: Peiligang millet farmers
events.descr: Cultivating millet and raising pigs, they make some of the oldest pottery in ancient China; their society is egalitarian. They are followed by the Yangshao culture.

events.title: Xinglongwa: the earliest ditched village in China
events.descr: Houses built in rows; 120 pit-houses at the type site. In the richest grave a man is buried with a pair of pigs and jade objects, and millet remains are found.

events.title: Hemudu: stilt houses and early rice
events.descr: One of the earliest rice-growing cultures; its people live in long stilt houses and make black pottery, carved jade, ivory, bone whistles and a red lacquer bowl.

events.title: Yangshao painted pottery (Banpo phase)
events.descr: Millet farmers who also grow some rice and raise pigs; they make white, red and black painted pottery. A dragon statue of the fifth millennium BC is the world’s oldest known dragon depiction. Scholars trace a line from Yangshao to the Longshan and Shang cultures.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Phases, Origins, Subsistence, Crafts and Social structure

events.title: Hongshan jade dragons
events.descr: Known for jade pig dragons and embryo dragons, among the earliest jade working; it interacts with the contemporary Yangshao, and its jades show considerable kinship with some Shang jades.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Historical context, Artifacts and Development of Chinese civilization

events.title: Dawenkou culture
events.descr: Turquoise, jade and ivory are common; the earliest alligator drums appear here. It co-exists with the Yangshao culture and has a lead role in generating Longshan.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Chronology and Interactions with other cultures

events.title: Early Jeulmun pit-house villages
events.descr: Small semi-permanent settlements with pit-houses. Gosan-ni pottery has been dated to 10,000 BC, though more dating is needed.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Incipient Jeulmun and Early Jeulmun

events.title: Domesticated peaches reach Jōmon Japan from China
events.descr: In the Early Jōmon, a period that saw an explosion in population. Jōmon pottery, decorated by impressing cords into wet clay, is among the oldest in the world.

sources.sourceLocation: Chronology, Early Jōmon, Early agriculture and Pottery

events.title: Kuk Swamp: drainage ditches and early agriculture
events.descr: One of the places where people independently developed agriculture; the native crop taro was grown, and drainage ditches date back to about 9,000 years ago.

events.title: Bananas and sugar cane planted at Kuk
events.descr: Eumusa bananas; a managed grassland of 6950–6550 years ago points to deliberate planting.

events.title: Plano bison hunters
events.descr: They hunted Bison antiquus, forcing stampedes off cliffs.

events.title: The oldest dogs in the Americas (Koster)
events.descr: Dog burials about 9,900 years old at one of the oldest known cemetery sites in eastern North America, occupied from the early Archaic (7500 BC).

events.title: Windover pond burials
events.descr: Hunter-gatherers bury their dead in the pond; brain tissue survives in 91 skulls, and graves hold woven palm-leaf fabrics and the earliest documented bottle gourd north of Mexico.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Site, Deposition, Textiles and Bags and containers

events.title: Squash domesticated at Guilá Naquitz
events.descr: The earliest known evidence for domestication of any crop on the continent: intentional breeding of squash (C. pepo) by no later than 8,000 years BP. Earlier AMS dates of 10,000 BP have been called into question.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Crop domestication and Timeline of domesticate changes

source.sourceLocation: Crop domestication ('no later than 8,000 years BP')

events.title: Maize domesticated in southern Mexico
events.descr: Domesticated by indigenous peoples from wild teosinte about 9,000 years ago.

events.title: Cueva de las Manos: the first paintings
events.descr: The oldest-known cave paintings in South America, made in several waves until AD 700 by hunters of guanacos.

events.title: Potatoes domesticated around Lake Titicaca
events.descr: In southern Peru and northwestern Bolivia, about 7,000–10,000 years ago.

events.title: Paloma, an early fishing village
events.descr: One of the earliest villages in the Americas dated stratigraphically; its diet was mainly fish and shellfish.

events.title: Huaca Prieta: early maize and dyed cotton
events.descr: Corncobs from Paredones and Huaca Prieta may date from as early as 4700 BCE (Dolores Piperno); dyed cotton fabric found in 2016 is about 6000 years old.

sources.sourceLocation: Early maize found and Early use of cotton and indigo dye

events.title: Karahan Tepe
events.descr: Possibly the earliest known human village. It lies in the same region as Göbekli Tepe, predates its construction by several centuries, and archaeologists believe the sites are related.

events.title: Nevalı Çori: temples and monumental sculpture
events.descr: Some of the world’s oldest known temples and monumental sculpture, in the Taş Tepeler tradition; similar structures are known only from Göbekli Tepe.

events.title: Aşıklı Höyük settled
events.descr: One of the earliest Aceramic Neolithic sites on the Anatolian plateau, considerably smaller than nearby Çatalhöyük.

events.title: Abu Hureyra: a farming village on the Euphrates
events.descr: One of the most important sites in the study of the origins of agriculture; its first domesticated cereals came about around 10,000 years ago, and basket weaving there dates back to 6500 BC.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Second occupation, Transition from foraging to farming and Agriculture

events.title: Byblos first settled
events.descr: In the Pre-Pottery Neolithic B; Byblos has been continuously inhabited since 5000 BC.

sources.sourceLocation: lead and Neolithic and Chalcolithic levels

events.title: Yarmukian culture
events.descr: A Pottery Neolithic A culture of the Levant, existing alongside the Lodian (Jericho IX) and Nizzanim cultures.

events.title: Jarmo, an early farming village
events.descr: An agricultural community contemporary with Jericho and Çatalhöyük, at its height between 6200 and 5800 BC; its art marks the inception of the Art of Mesopotamia.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, The village and Pottery and religion

events.title: Tell Brak settled
events.descr: The earliest small settlement belongs to the proto-Halaf culture; Halaf and Northern Ubaid phases follow.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, history table and Early settlement

events.title: Tell Brak becomes one of the first cities
events.descr: Urbanisation begins in the late 5th millennium BCE; in Period E (c. 4200–3900 BC) the city’s walls are built, and by early Period F (c. 3800–3600 BC) it covers 130 hectares. It is one of the earliest known cities in the world; later an Urukean colony is established there.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Brak Period E and Brak Period F

events.title: Ounjougou: the earliest pottery in Africa
events.descr: Before 9400 BCE Niger-Congo speakers independently created and used mature ceramic technology; the pottery makers later migrate, and pottery at Bir Kiseiba in Egypt resembles Ounjougou’s.

source.sourceLocation: Early Holocene ('during the first half of the 10th millennium BC')

events.title: Early Khartoum pottery makers
events.descr: From a time before food production began in Africa; sites in Sudan such as Esh Shaheinab are some of the earliest examples of pottery-making in Africa.

sources.sourceLocation: lead ('Early Khartoum (8800 to 5000 BP)') and Pottery

events.title: The Pesse canoe, the world’s oldest known boat
events.descr: Made in the early Mesolithic.

events.title: Doggerland floods: Britain is cut off
events.descr: Rising seas inundate Doggerland between 10,000 and 7,000 years ago, cutting the British peninsula off from the mainland by around 6500 BCE; Dogger Bank remains an island until at least 5000 BCE. Doggerland may have been Europe’s most prosperous hunting, fowling and fishing ground in the Mesolithic.

events.title: The Storegga Slide tsunami
events.descr: Structural failures of the continental shelf cause underwater landslides and a tsunami in the North Atlantic; one hypothesis holds that it flooded much of Doggerland’s remaining coast.

events.title: Ertebølle hunter-fishers make pottery
events.descr: A hunter-gatherer and fisher culture of the end of the Mesolithic, roughly contemporary with the Linear Pottery culture; shortly after 4,100 BCE it spreads along the Baltic coast, and it is then replaced by the Funnelbeaker culture.

events.title: Hamangia culture: “The Thinker”
events.descr: Known for exceptional clay figures, including The Thinker and Sitting Woman (c. 4900 BC); it is followed by the Varna culture.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, Genesis and successor, Art and Gallery

events.title: Dimini culture: abstract painted vessels
events.descr: Characteristic of the Later Neolithic in eastern Thessaly. An "invasion theory" has it conquering the Sesklo culture around 5000 BC; Lyritzis’s thermoluminescence dates instead show it appearing about 4800 BC, four centuries before Sesklo’s end.

events.title: The Goseck circle
events.descr: Perhaps the oldest and best known of the circular enclosures of the Central European Neolithic, probably a ritual or cult structure; it dates to the transition from Linear Pottery to Stroke-ornamented ware.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, History and Astronomical alignment

events.title: Lengyel culture: the dawn of the Chalcolithic in Central Europe
events.descr: Copper beads and ribbons mark the dawn of the Chalcolithic in Central Europe. It follows the Linear Pottery culture and overlaps the Funnelbeaker culture.

events.title: Michelsberg culture
events.descr: Undecorated tulip beakers, hilltop settlements and enclosures; it emerges in northeastern France and plays an instrumental role in establishing the Funnelbeaker culture. Its Kapellenberg tumulus shows the influence of the Castellic culture of Brittany.

events.title: Barnenez cairn
events.descr: One of the earliest megalithic monuments in Europe, remarkable for its megalithic art; built in two phases (4850–4250 and 4450–4000 BC).

events.title: Knap of Howar, the oldest stone house in northern Europe
events.descr: It may be the oldest preserved stone house in northern Europe, earlier than the similar houses at Skara Brae.

events.title: Bacsonian culture
events.descr: Part of the Hoabinhian, a lithic techno-complex. At Spirit Cave in Thailand, Gorman claimed early plant remains, but Higham and Thosarat find no grounds for linking the site with agriculture; it has no ceramics until after 6800 BCE (Solheim).

events.title: Cishan millet farmers
events.descr: Farming of broomcorn millet, stored in over 500 pits; pigs are the main source of meat, and nets are made of hemp. Dates of 10,000 years ago for its millet have been questioned. It is followed by the Yangshao culture.

events.title: Houli culture in Shandong
events.descr: Rice, broomcorn millet and foxtail millet are found at its sites (rice at Yuezhang AMS-dated to 8010–7700 BP, not confirmed as domesticated); people live in square semi-subterranean houses and rely mostly on hunting and fishing.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Archaeological findings and Yuezhang

events.title: Daxi culture: rice and walled settlements
events.descr: The Daxi people cultivate rice extensively, and their sites are some of the earliest in China with moats and walled settlements.

events.title: Majiabang culture: paddy rice and jade
events.descr: Paddy fields at Caoxieshan and Chuodun; jade ornaments, and a wooden scull and oar. It coexists with the Hemudu culture and is succeeded by the Liangzhu culture.

events.title: Caverna da Pedra Pintada: the earliest cave paintings in the Americas
events.descr: Human presence about 11,200 to 10,000 years ago, with spear points and Brazil nuts; its paintings are the earliest known cave paintings in the Americas.

events.title: The Spirit Cave mummy
events.descr: The oldest human mummy found in North America, wrapped in a rabbit-skin blanket and woven tule matting.
